title: The Bank Call
message: A caller says they are from your bank. They know your name and the last four digits of your account. They say a suspicious transfer is happening and ask for the OTP that just arrived on your phone.
options: Give the OTP
Hang up and call the bank using a trusted number
Ask the caller to send another code
lesson: Partial knowledge does not prove identity. One-time codes are not something an unexpected caller should receive.

title: 10 Minutes
message: A text says: “Your account will be permanently blocked in 10 minutes. Verify now.” A link is included.
options: Click immediately
Pause and verify through the official app/site
Forward it to a friend
lesson: Urgency is a lever. Breaking the sender's communication path gives you time to verify.

title: Safe Account
message: Someone claiming to be an investigator says your account is connected to a crime. They demand that you transfer your money to a “safe account” immediately.
options: Transfer the money
Ask for a badge number and comply
Do not transfer; independently verify the claim
lesson: Threats and authority claims should make you verify, not surrender control of your money.

title: Is This You?
message: A friend's account sends: “Is this you in this video? 😂” followed by an unfamiliar link. The message is unusual for them.
options: Open the link
Verify with the friend through another channel
Ask them to resend it
lesson: Familiar accounts can be compromised. Verify unexpected links before opening them.

title: The Millionaire Prize
message: You receive a message saying you won ₦5,000,000. To release it, you must pay a ₦25,000 processing fee within 20 minutes.
options: Pay the fee
Send your ID first
Stop and treat the fee demand as a major scam signal
lesson: Unexpected prizes plus upfront fees are a classic fraud pattern.

title: Hospital Emergency
message: A person you met online says their child is in hospital and urgently asks for ₦50,000. They say refusing means you do not care.
options: Send immediately
Verify the identity and story independently
Borrow money for them
lesson: Compassion is good. Verification keeps compassion from being exploited.

title: Changed Supplier
message: An email from a supplier says their bank account has changed and asks you to pay today's ₦850,000 invoice to a new account immediately.
options: Pay the new account
Verify using a previously known contact method
Reply asking if the change is real
lesson: Payment changes should be verified outside the channel that requested the change.

title: AI Voice
message: You receive a voice note that sounds exactly like a family member. They say they lost their phone and need money urgently. The number is unfamiliar.
options: Send the money
Verify through a known number or trusted channel
Ask for a voice note proving it
lesson: A convincing voice is no longer strong identity proof. Change channel and verify.

title: Fake Support
message: You complain about your bank on social media. An account using the bank's logo replies and asks you to DM your PIN and OTP so they can “fix” the issue.
options: Send the details
Use the bank's official app/site support
Send only the PIN
lesson: Use official support channels. Legitimate support should not need your password, PIN or OTP.

title: The QR Reward
message: A poster says: “Scan to claim your reward.” The QR code opens a page asking for your banking login.
options: Log in
Close it and navigate to the official service yourself
Enter the password but not the OTP
lesson: QR codes are just links in another form. Inspect the destination and verify it.

title: Your Account Is Hacked
message: You notice login alerts from a device you do not recognise and your password no longer works. What should you do first?
options: Keep trying the old password
Use the service's official recovery/security process and secure the account from a trusted device
Message the person who changed it
Post your password online asking for help
lesson: Treat unexpected login alerts and password changes as an incident. Use the official recovery route, secure the account, review sessions and change reused passwords.

title: Block It Now
message: You think someone may have access to your bank account. A stranger online gives you a number and says it is the fastest way to block your account. What is safest?
options: Call the stranger's number immediately
Use your bank's official app, website, card documentation or verified customer-service/fraud channel
Give the stranger your PIN so they can block it
Search social media comments for another random number
lesson: There is no single universal bank-blocking number that is safe to trust across all banks. Use the official channel published by your own bank and report suspected fraud immediately.

title: SIM Swap Warning
message: Your phone suddenly loses network service. Minutes later, you receive an email about a password reset you did not request.
options: Wait until the network returns
Contact your mobile network through an official channel and your financial providers through verified channels
Post your OTP on social media to ask what happened
Try every password you have used before
lesson: Unexpected loss of mobile service combined with account alerts can indicate SIM-swap or account takeover. Contact the network and affected providers through trusted channels quickly.

title: The Recovery Code
message: A person claiming to be platform support says they can recover your account if you send them the recovery code that just arrived by SMS.
options: Send the code
Ask for their employee ID and send the code
Do not share it; use the platform's official recovery process
Send half of the code
lesson: Recovery codes are credentials. Never disclose them to someone who contacts you unexpectedly.

title: The Fake Refund
message: A seller says they accidentally refunded you twice and asks you to send one refund back to a different account immediately.
options: Send it immediately
Verify the transaction independently and resolve the refund through the original payment channel
Send a smaller amount first
Ask for their bank PIN
lesson: Do not rush a payment reversal to a new destination. Verify the original transaction and use the legitimate payment platform's process.

title: The Job Offer
message: A recruiter offers you a remote job with unusually high pay. Before an interview, they ask you to pay for a 'mandatory activation package' through a personal account.
options: Pay quickly to secure the job
Verify the company independently and refuse unexplained upfront payments
Send your banking password instead
Borrow money to pay the fee
lesson: Upfront fees, personal payment accounts and pressure before basic verification are major job-scam signals.

title: The Landlord Changed Number
message: You are about to pay ₦1.8m rent. The person handling the property says their phone was stolen and sends a new bank account for payment. The agent is not answering.
options: Pay because the message has the correct property address
Pause and independently verify the account and property representative before paying
Send a token first
Ask the new number to confirm the OTP
lesson: Payment-account changes for high-value transactions need independent verification using a previously trusted contact or in-person channel.

title: The CEO Voice Note
message: Your CEO sends a voice note asking you to urgently buy gift cards for a client and send the codes. The request is unusual and arrives from a new number.
options: Buy them immediately
Verify the request through a known company channel before acting
Send the codes but hide the receipts
Reply asking which gift cards they prefer
lesson: Authority plus urgency is a classic business-impersonation pattern. Verify unusual financial requests out of band.

title: QR Login Trap
message: A QR code in a message says it will secure your account. After scanning, the page asks you to enter your username, password and OTP.
options: Enter everything
Enter only the username
Close it and open the official app/site directly
Take a screenshot and send it to the sender
lesson: A QR code does not make a destination trustworthy. Never surrender credentials to an unexpected page; navigate independently to the official service.

title: Crypto Recovery Expert
message: After losing money on an investment platform, someone claiming to be a recovery expert contacts you and promises to recover the funds for a fee. They ask for remote access to your laptop.
options: Give remote access
Pay the fee
Stop and verify the service independently; never give remote control or credentials
Send them your wallet password
lesson: Recovery scams target people who have already suffered losses. Remote access and credential requests can create a second compromise.

title: The Deepfake Meeting
message: In a video call, a senior executive appears to ask you to approve an urgent transfer. The video freezes twice and they insist there is no time for a callback.
options: Approve because you saw their face
Ask for a second trusted verification channel and follow payment controls
Approve half now
Send the approval code in chat
lesson: A convincing face or voice is not sufficient proof of identity. High-value transfers should follow established verification and approval controls.

title: The WhatsApp Takeover
message: A friend says their WhatsApp account was locked and asks you to forward a six-digit code that just arrived on your phone.
options: Forward it
Read only the first three digits
Do not share it; verify with your friend through another channel
Send a screenshot of the SMS
lesson: Unexpected verification-code requests can be an attempt to take over your account. Verification codes belong only to the account holder.

title: The Scholarship Portal
message: A scholarship advert says applications close tonight and asks for a 'verification fee' plus your banking login to confirm eligibility.
options: Pay and apply
Use the programme's independently verified official website and never provide banking credentials
Send only the password
Ask the advert account for an OTP
lesson: Scholarship scams often combine urgency, fees and requests for sensitive information. Verify the programme through an independent official source.

title: The Marketplace Buyer
message: A buyer says they have paid for your item and sends a screenshot of a bank transfer. They ask you to release the item before the funds appear in your account.
options: Release the item
Wait for the payment to be independently confirmed in your own account/payment system
Send the item and trust the screenshot
Refund the buyer first
lesson: Screenshots are not proof of settlement. Verify payment through your own trusted account or payment platform before releasing goods.

title: The Fake Police Threat
message: A caller claims to be police and says you must immediately pay a fine through a personal bank account or face arrest tonight.
options: Pay immediately
End the call and independently verify the claim through official channels
Give your BVN for identification
Ask the caller to send an OTP
lesson: Real authority claims should be independently verifiable. Threats combined with immediate personal-account payments are strong warning signs.

title: The Password Reuse Chain
message: You discover that an old shopping site you used suffered a breach. You reused that password on your email and banking-related services.
options: Do nothing because the breach is old
Change reused passwords, starting with email, and enable MFA where available
Post the old password to see if it still works
Wait for a suspicious transaction
lesson: Password reuse turns one breach into multiple account risks. Change reused passwords and protect your most important accounts first.

title: The Support Screen Share
message: A pop-up says your computer is infected and gives a phone number. The caller asks you to install remote-control software so they can fix it.
options: Install it
Give them remote access but stay on the call
Close the pop-up and seek help through a trusted support route
Send them your antivirus password
lesson: Unexpected technical-support calls and remote-access requests are common scam patterns. Use trusted support channels instead.

title: The Insider Request
message: A colleague asks you to bypass the normal two-person approval process because the CFO is travelling and the payment is 'extremely urgent.'
options: Bypass the control
Follow the normal approval process and independently verify the request
Approve because the colleague is trusted
Send the approval token to the colleague
lesson: Security controls exist for stressful moments. Urgency is not a reason to bypass established approval procedures.

title: The Account Recovery Link
message: An email says your cloud account was accessed from another country. The button opens a login page whose domain is almost—but not exactly—the real service domain.
options: Log in quickly
Check the domain carefully and navigate to the service independently
Enter the password and skip MFA
Forward the email to the sender for confirmation
lesson: Lookalike domains can imitate trusted services. Avoid the supplied login link and access the service through a trusted route.

title: The Emergency Family Transfer
message: You receive a voice call that sounds like your sibling. They claim they are stranded and need ₦300,000 within five minutes. They beg you not to call anyone.
options: Transfer immediately
Use a pre-agreed family verification method or call a known number before sending money
Ask them to repeat your sibling's name
Send half first
lesson: AI can imitate familiar voices. A trusted verification method beats voice familiarity when money and urgency are involved.

title: The Wrong Account
message: A stranger says a transfer was accidentally sent to your account. They ask you to send the money to a different account because their original account is 'not working'.
options: Send it to the new account immediately
Leave the money untouched and contact your bank through an official channel
Keep the money because it was sent to you
Ask the stranger for your OTP first
lesson: Unexpected incoming money can be linked to fraud. Do not move it on your own. Notify your bank and let the legitimate financial process handle the reversal.

title: Use My Account
message: Someone you know says they have reached their daily transfer limit and asks you to receive a large payment into your account for them, promising to give you cash afterward.
options: Agree because you know the person
Refuse to receive unexplained funds and advise them to use their own legitimate banking channel
Receive it and forward it elsewhere
Receive it but withdraw the money immediately
lesson: Allowing others to route unexplained money through your account can expose you to serious financial and legal risk. Keep your account for legitimate transactions you understand.

title: The Refund Middleman
message: A buyer says they accidentally paid you from someone else's account and asks you to refund the 'extra' payment to a third account rather than the original payer.
options: Refund the third account
Pause and have the payment provider or bank resolve the transaction
Send the refund in cash
Use another person's account to refund it
lesson: A refund should be resolved through the original payment trail or a trusted provider. Sending funds to an unrelated account can make you part of a money-moving chain.

title: The Charity Collector
message: A social-media account claims to be collecting donations for a child and posts emotional photos. It asks donors to transfer money to a personal account and says there is no time to verify.
options: Send immediately
Verify the charity, beneficiary and payment details independently before donating
Share the post with everyone first
Ask the collector for your card PIN
lesson: Emotional stories can be genuine or manipulated. Verify the organisation and beneficiary independently before sending money.

title: The Job Equipment Fee
message: A recruiter offers you a remote job and says you must pay ₦40,000 for a laptop registration and background-check certificate before receiving the contract.
options: Pay because the salary is attractive
Verify the employer independently and treat an unexpected upfront payment demand as a warning sign
Send your banking password instead
Borrow the money and pay quickly
lesson: Fraudulent job offers often use attractive opportunities to justify fees or requests for sensitive information. Verify the employer through an independent route.

title: The Rental Deposit
message: A landlord's supposed agent says a beautiful apartment will be given to whoever pays the full rent deposit tonight. They refuse inspection and insist on a personal account.
options: Pay immediately
Verify ownership/agency, inspect the property and independently confirm payment details before paying
Send a smaller deposit to reserve it
Give them your bank login to prove you can pay
lesson: Property fraud often combines scarcity with large upfront payments. Verify the property, owner/agent and payment destination before transferring funds.

title: The Investment Recovery Agent
message: After losing money on an online investment, someone claiming to be a recovery agent contacts you and promises to recover it if you first pay a 'release tax'.
options: Pay the release tax
Stop and independently verify the service; do not send more money to recover money you already lost
Give them remote access to your phone
Send your card details so they can process the recovery
lesson: Recovery scams target people who have already been harmed. A new fee is not proof that recovery is legitimate.

title: The Crypto Wallet Helper
message: A stranger offers to help recover your crypto wallet and asks for your seed phrase so they can 'restore' the funds.
options: Send the seed phrase
Never share the seed phrase; use official wallet recovery guidance
Send half the words
Take a screenshot and send it
lesson: A wallet seed phrase is highly sensitive. Legitimate support should not need you to disclose it.

title: The Verification Deposit
message: A person claiming to verify your identity says they will send a small amount into your account, but first asks you to transfer ₦1,000 to prove the account is active.
options: Send the ₦1,000
Verify the organisation independently and use its official verification process
Send your OTP instead
Let them log in to your banking app
lesson: A small payment request can still be a fraud test. Verify the organisation and never surrender banking credentials.

title: The Fake Delivery Fee
message: A text says your parcel is held at customs and requires a small delivery fee through a link. You are not expecting a parcel.
options: Pay because the fee is small
Do not use the link; verify the parcel through the delivery company's official channel
Enter your card details but not the OTP
Reply with your address
lesson: Small fees can be used to steal payment details or credentials. An unexpected delivery should be verified independently.

title: The Fake Electricity Agent
message: Someone claiming to be a utility official says your power connection will be disconnected today unless you transfer payment to a personal account.
options: Pay immediately
Verify the bill and payment channel through the utility's official contact or portal
Send your meter PIN
Give the caller remote access to your phone
lesson: Threats of immediate service loss are designed to rush decisions. Verify bills and payment channels through official sources.

title: The SIM Registration Fix
message: A caller says your SIM registration has a problem and asks for your national identification details plus an OTP to 'update' it immediately.
options: Provide everything
End the call and contact your mobile network through an official channel
Send only the OTP
Ask the caller to try again tomorrow
lesson: Identity details and OTPs can be used for account takeover. Verify SIM-related requests through your network provider's official channel.

title: The New Number
message: A relative messages from a new number saying their phone broke. They ask you to save the new number and send money immediately.
options: Send immediately
Call the relative using the old known number or another trusted family contact to verify
Ask them for a selfie
Send a small amount first
lesson: A new number is not identity proof. Use a known channel to verify before sending money.

title: The Voice Clone
message: A voice call sounds like your manager and instructs you to transfer company funds urgently. The caller says they cannot join the normal approval process.
options: Transfer because the voice is familiar
Follow normal approval controls and verify through a known channel
Ask the caller to repeat the request louder
Send the approval code by SMS
lesson: AI can imitate voices. Financial requests must follow established verification and approval controls even when the voice sounds familiar.

title: The Fake Account Manager
message: A message says a new account manager has been assigned to you and asks you to confirm your PIN in a chat so they can activate premium banking services.
options: Send the PIN
Use the bank's official app or contact channel and never disclose the PIN
Send the PIN with the last digit hidden
Ask for their personal number
lesson: PINs are credentials. Premium services do not justify giving your PIN to an unexpected contact.

title: The OTP Test
message: Someone says they are helping you cancel a suspicious transaction. They ask you to read out the OTP that arrives so the cancellation can succeed.
options: Read the OTP
End the conversation and use the bank's official transaction-dispute or fraud channel
Forward the OTP to a friend
Ask for another OTP
lesson: An OTP can authorise an action rather than cancel one. Never disclose it to an unsolicited caller.

title: The Fake KYC Update
message: A message says your account's KYC will expire today and links to a form asking for your ID number, card details and password.
options: Fill it immediately
Open the official service yourself and verify whether any KYC action is actually required
Send only your password
Forward the form to coworkers
lesson: KYC requests can be impersonated. Verify the requirement through the institution's official channel before submitting identity or banking information.

title: The Fake Tax Officer
message: A caller claims your business has an unpaid tax penalty and demands payment into a personal account within one hour to avoid prosecution.
options: Pay immediately
Verify the assessment and payment instructions through the relevant official government channel
Send your bank login to prove cooperation
Transfer to a colleague's account
lesson: Government-payment claims should be independently verified. Personal accounts and extreme deadlines are warning signs.

title: The Grant Registration
message: A social-media page advertises a government grant and asks you to pay a registration fee before your name can be added to the beneficiary list.
options: Pay the fee
Verify the programme through the government's official channels before providing money or information
Send your ATM PIN
Ask the page for an OTP
lesson: Scammers frequently use government names and logos. Verify grants through independently reached official channels.

title: The Fake Exam Result
message: A message claims your exam result is withheld and asks you to pay a fee through a link to unlock it immediately.
options: Pay through the link
Access the institution's official portal directly and verify your result status
Send your password to the sender
Share your student ID publicly
lesson: Use the official portal you already know rather than a link supplied in an unexpected message.

title: The Marketplace Overpayment
message: A buyer says they accidentally transferred ₦500,000 instead of ₦50,000 and sends a screenshot. They ask you to return the difference before the payment appears in your account.
options: Return the difference immediately
Wait for independent confirmation and resolve the transaction through the trusted payment channel
Send the difference to another account
Withdraw cash and hand it over
lesson: Do not rely on payment screenshots or pressure. Confirm funds in your own account and resolve discrepancies through the payment provider.

title: The Fake Escrow
message: A buyer insists you use an unfamiliar escrow website they provide. The site asks you to log in with your bank credentials to receive payment.
options: Log in
Use only a trusted marketplace/payment service and never enter bank credentials into an unfamiliar site
Enter your password but not OTP
Ask the buyer to send their password
lesson: An unfamiliar escrow page can be a phishing site. Payment protection should not require you to hand banking credentials to a stranger.

title: The Business Invoice PDF
message: An email from a familiar supplier contains a new invoice PDF. The bank details differ from every previous invoice, but the email thread looks normal.
options: Pay because the email thread is familiar
Verify the bank-detail change using a previously trusted contact method
Reply to the same email asking for confirmation
Pay half first
lesson: Compromised email accounts can make fraudulent messages look legitimate. Verify changed payment details outside the email thread.

title: The Executive's WhatsApp
message: A WhatsApp account using your director's name and photo asks you to buy gift cards for a client and send the codes immediately.
options: Buy and send them
Verify the request using a known company channel and follow established purchasing controls
Send one code as a test
Ask the account for a voice note
lesson: Names, photos and voice notes do not prove identity. Verify unusual financial requests through established business channels.

title: The Password Reset Bomb
message: You receive many password-reset emails you did not request, followed by a call from someone asking for the reset code so they can 'stop the attack'.
options: Give the code to stop the attacker
Do not share the code; secure the account using the official service and review security settings
Ignore everything forever
Send the code to your email contact
lesson: Attackers can trigger reset messages to pressure you into revealing the code. Use the official security process instead.

title: The Browser Warning
message: A website displays a full-screen warning saying your device is infected and tells you to call a support number immediately.
options: Call the number
Close the page and use trusted security/support tools; do not rely on the pop-up's phone number
Install whatever software the caller recommends
Give the caller remote access
lesson: Scareware uses alarming messages to make you call fake support. Do not trust contact details displayed by an untrusted page.

title: The Fake Antivirus
message: A download page says your antivirus has expired and offers a free replacement. The installer asks for administrator access and disables your existing protection.
options: Install it
Cancel and obtain security software only from a trusted official source
Disable your antivirus first
Send the installer to friends
lesson: Unexpected security software prompts can be malware. Use trusted sources and be suspicious of software that asks to disable existing protection.

title: The USB Gift
message: A stranger leaves a USB drive labelled 'Salary List' in your office and someone suggests plugging it into the work computer to see who it belongs to.
options: Plug it in
Do not connect unknown removable media; follow your organisation's security process
Plug it into a personal laptop instead
Open it on the office network
lesson: Unknown removable media can introduce malware. Use established handling procedures rather than testing it yourself.

title: The Public Wi-Fi Login
message: At a café, a Wi-Fi network named exactly like the café's network asks you to enter your email password to connect.
options: Enter your email password
Confirm the network details with staff and avoid entering important account passwords into a captive portal you do not trust
Use your banking password instead
Share the password with other customers
lesson: Lookalike networks can capture information. Confirm the network and avoid exposing sensitive credentials.

title: The Free Charging Cable
message: A stranger offers you a free charging cable at an event and says it charges phones faster. You are asked to connect it to your unlocked phone.
options: Use it immediately
Use your own trusted charger/cable or a power bank
Connect it while sharing your PIN
Use it only for banking
lesson: Unknown accessories can create device risks. Use trusted charging equipment, especially with sensitive devices.

title: The Lost Phone
message: You lose your phone that has email, banking and social apps signed in. You can still access your accounts from another device.
options: Wait a few days
Use trusted account/device-management tools to secure the phone, change important credentials and contact your providers as needed
Post all your passwords publicly
Ignore the loss if the SIM has a PIN
lesson: A lost device can expose active sessions. Secure it remotely where possible and protect important accounts promptly.

title: The Stolen Laptop
message: A work laptop is stolen from your car. It contains company documents and may have saved browser sessions.
options: Wait to see if it returns
Report the theft immediately and follow the organisation's device/account incident process
Change only the laptop wallpaper
Tell nobody to avoid embarrassment
lesson: Lost devices can expose data and active sessions. Prompt reporting allows accounts, devices and data to be protected.

title: The Fake Login QR
message: At a conference, a QR code labelled 'Free Wi-Fi' opens a login page that resembles your email provider and asks for your password.
options: Enter the password
Use the official network instructions and avoid entering credentials into an unexpected QR-linked page
Use your email password just once
Take a photo of the page and send it to a stranger
lesson: QR codes can lead to phishing pages. Treat them like any other untrusted link and verify the destination.

title: The Deepfake Meeting
message: During a video call, a supposed senior executive asks you to approve a confidential payment. The face and voice look convincing, but the request is unusual and outside the normal process.
options: Approve because you saw the person live
Stop and verify through a known channel and follow normal approval procedures
Record the meeting and approve later without checking
Send your login details to the executive
lesson: Realistic video is not proof of identity. High-risk financial requests need independent verification and established controls.

title: The Fake Security Team
message: A message from 'Cybersecurity Team' says your account is under attack and asks you to install a remote-access app so they can secure it.
options: Install it
Contact your organisation's security team through a known internal channel
Give them temporary access
Send a screenshot of your passwords
lesson: Security teams can be impersonated too. Use known internal contact details rather than trusting an unexpected message.

title: The Cloud Storage Share
message: You receive a shared-document notification from a colleague. The document asks you to sign in again, but the sign-in domain is unfamiliar.
options: Log in
Verify the share with the colleague and access the service through its official site/app
Enter the password and skip MFA
Forward the login page
lesson: Shared documents can be used as phishing lures. Verify the message and domain before signing in.

title: The Social Media Blue Tick
message: A verified-looking social account offers to recover your suspended page for a fee and asks for your login code.
options: Pay and send the code
Use the platform's official appeal/recovery process
Send only the username and code
Give them your backup email password
lesson: Badges and professional-looking profiles can be imitated or abused. Use the platform's official recovery path.

title: The Giveaway Winner
message: A celebrity-looking page announces that you won a phone and asks you to pay delivery charges through a personal account.
options: Pay the delivery fee
Verify the giveaway through the celebrity/brand's independently reached official channels
Send your card details
Share your OTP
lesson: Celebrity and brand impersonation can make fake giveaways look credible. Verify independently before paying or sharing information.

title: The Romance Investment
message: Someone you have been talking to online says they made money trading and offers to invest your money for you. They ask you to transfer funds to an account they control.
options: Send the money
Keep financial control, independently verify any investment service and never give a stranger control of your funds
Send your banking password instead
Borrow money to invest more
lesson: Romance can be used to create trust before financial requests. Keep control of your money and verify investment services independently.

title: The Sextortion Threat
message: A stranger threatens to publish private images unless you pay immediately. They demand cryptocurrency and say payment will make the threat disappear.
options: Pay immediately
Do not negotiate by sending money; preserve evidence and seek appropriate platform, legal or support assistance
Send more images as proof
Give them your account password
lesson: Payment does not guarantee a threat will stop. Preserve evidence, secure accounts and seek appropriate support rather than giving the extortionist more access.

title: The Fake Loan Approval
message: A lender says your loan is approved instantly but requires an 'insurance fee' before releasing the funds. The lender has no verifiable office or official website.
options: Pay the fee
Verify the lender independently and be cautious of upfront-payment demands
Send your ATM PIN
Allow them to log into your account
lesson: Loan scams often promise easy approval and then demand fees. Verify lenders independently before paying or sharing financial information.

title: The Debt Collector
message: A caller claims you owe a debt and threatens arrest unless you pay into a personal account within 30 minutes. You do not recognise the debt.
options: Pay to be safe
Request verifiable details and independently confirm the debt through the legitimate organisation
Give your BVN to prove identity
Transfer to a different personal account
lesson: Fear and authority can be used to force payment. Verify the debt and payment channel independently.

title: The SIM Replacement Agent
message: A person says your SIM replacement is ready and asks you to confirm a code sent to your phone. You did not request a replacement.
options: Give the code
Do not share it; contact your network provider through an official channel immediately
Send the code to your bank instead
Ignore the code but keep chatting
lesson: An unexpected SIM replacement can be a serious warning. Do not disclose verification codes; contact the network provider through a trusted route.

title: The Password Manager Export
message: Someone claiming to be IT support asks you to export all saved passwords from your password manager and email the file for troubleshooting.
options: Send the file
Refuse to export or email credentials; use the approved IT/security support process
Remove only banking passwords and send the rest
Zip the file with a simple password
lesson: A password export can expose many accounts at once. Legitimate support should use approved secure procedures, not ask you to email credential stores.

title: The Browser Autofill Trap
message: A shopping site looks familiar and your browser offers to autofill your saved card information. The address contains an extra word you did not expect.
options: Accept autofill
Stop and verify the exact domain before entering or autofilling sensitive payment information
Use a different card and continue
Enter the CVV only
lesson: Autofill can make phishing easier. Check the exact website address before submitting sensitive information.

title: The Friend's Fundraiser
message: A friend's social account suddenly starts fundraising for a medical emergency. The writing style is unusual and the payment account belongs to someone else.
options: Donate immediately
Contact the friend through a known channel and verify the fundraiser
Share the post first
Ask the account for an OTP
lesson: Compromised accounts can be used to exploit existing relationships. Verify unusual financial requests through another channel.

title: The Data Broker Form

title: The Payment Approval Gap
message: Your finance team discovers there is no dual-approval requirement for wire transfers above ₦5,000,000 — one person alone can approve and send. What do you do?
options: Leave it as is since it hasn't caused a problem yet
Implement mandatory dual-approval for transfers above the threshold immediately
Add dual-approval only for transfers above ₦50,000,000
Ask the finance lead to informally double-check without a formal policy
lesson: A single point of approval for high-value transfers is exactly the gap business email compromise scams exploit. Formal dual-approval closes it structurally, not just by trusting one person's vigilance.

title: The Shared Login
message: Your team has been sharing one login for the company's accounting software for years because it's 'simpler'. What's the right move?
options: Continue sharing it since it's convenient
Move to individual accounts with role-based access and enable MFA
Change the shared password monthly instead of individual accounts
Only share it with senior staff
lesson: Shared logins make it impossible to know who did what, and a single leaked password compromises everyone. Individual accounts with MFA fix both problems at once.

title: The Ex-Employee's Access
message: An employee resigned three weeks ago, but IT never received a formal offboarding request, so their access to email and internal systems is still active.
options: Wait until IT does its routine cleanup
Immediately revoke all access as part of a formal offboarding checklist
Just disable email but leave other systems
Ask the employee to confirm they've stopped using the accounts
lesson: Access should be revoked the moment someone leaves, not whenever it's convenient. A formal offboarding checklist makes this automatic instead of dependent on someone remembering.

title: The New Vendor
message: Your company is about to start paying a new vendor. There's currently no process to verify a vendor's bank details before the first payment.
options: Pay based on the details in their invoice
Verify the vendor's bank details through an independent channel — a phone call to a known contact, not the invoice — before the first payment
Ask the vendor to confirm their own details twice by email
Only verify for vendors above a certain contract size
lesson: Invoices can be intercepted or spoofed. Verifying bank details through a separate, independently-confirmed channel before the first payment is the single control that stops most vendor-fraud losses.

title: The Password Policy
message: An internal audit finds that most staff reuse the same password across multiple work systems, and there's no minimum password policy.
options: Leave individual staff to manage their own passwords
Introduce a password manager, a unique-password policy, and MFA across all work systems
Just ask staff nicely to use stronger passwords
Force a password change only once a year
lesson: One reused password leaking anywhere compromises every system it's used on. A password manager plus MFA removes the temptation to reuse passwords in the first place.

title: The Public Wi-Fi Habit
message: Several staff regularly handle company email and files over public Wi-Fi at cafes, with no VPN requirement in place.
options: Allow it since it hasn't caused an issue
Require a company VPN for any work done over public networks
Ask staff to avoid email specifically on public Wi-Fi
Only restrict this for senior staff who handle sensitive data
lesson: Public networks make it easier to intercept unencrypted traffic. A VPN requirement is a simple, low-friction control that closes this gap for everyone, not just some staff.

title: The Phishing Report Culture
message: Staff who click suspicious links tend to stay quiet about it out of embarrassment, and there's no simple way to report a possible phishing email.
options: Leave it — most staff figure it out eventually
Set up a simple, no-blame reporting channel and normalize reporting early
Only address it after an actual incident occurs
Send an annual reminder email about phishing
lesson: A culture where people are afraid to report a mistake delays the response to a real incident by hours or days. A no-blame reporting channel gets IT involved while there's still time to limit the damage.

title: The Unpatched Software
message: IT discovers that critical software across the office hasn't been updated in several months because updates 'might disrupt work'.
options: Continue delaying updates to avoid disruption
Schedule regular, tested update windows so security patches are applied promptly
Update only when something visibly breaks
Update only the software that handles payments
lesson: Unpatched software is one of the most common ways attackers get in — the vulnerability is often public knowledge. Scheduled, tested update windows balance stability with actually closing known holes.

title: The Personal Device Policy
message: Staff routinely use personal phones and laptops to access company email and documents, with no formal device security policy in place.
options: Continue allowing it freely
Introduce a bring-your-own-device policy requiring basic security — passcode, encryption, remote wipe capability — before access is granted
Ban personal devices entirely without an alternative
Only apply a policy to devices used by management
lesson: A lost or stolen personal phone with company email on it is a data breach waiting to happen. A BYOD policy with baseline security requirements protects company data without banning convenience outright.

title: The Backup Gap
message: Your company backs up files automatically, but nobody has ever tested whether those backups can actually be restored.
options: Assume the backups are fine since they run on schedule
Regularly test restoring from backup to confirm it actually works
Only test backups after a major incident
Add more backup frequency instead of testing restoration
lesson: A backup that has never been tested is not a real backup plan — it's a hope. Ransomware recovery specifically depends on backups that are verified to actually restore, not just exist.

title: The Social Media Access
message: Several former employees and contractors still technically have login access to the company's social media accounts.
options: Leave it since they probably won't misuse it
Immediately revoke their access and rotate the account passwords as a standard offboarding step
Only worry about it if something goes wrong
Just remove them as 'admin' but leave other access levels
lesson: Public-facing accounts left open to former staff or contractors are a reputational risk, not just a security one. Revoking access and rotating credentials should be a standard, automatic offboarding step.

title: The Incident Response Plan
message: Your organization has never actually written down who does what if a cyberattack or data breach happens — it's assumed people will 'figure it out'.
options: Continue without a formal plan since nothing has happened yet
Create and periodically rehearse a written incident response plan naming clear roles and responsibilities
Write a plan but never test or update it
Assign incident response informally to whoever is available at the time
lesson: During a real incident is the worst time to figure out who's in charge of what. A written, rehearsed plan turns a chaotic first hour into a manageable, practiced response.
